1:
The title is explained topographically, then theologically. John Gill takes the valley of vision for Jerusalem, ringed with mountains and home of the seers, and hears an allusion to the city's name, the vision of peace. Matthew Henry adds a second sense: fitly a valley, since by God's judgments a people once a towering mountain should be brought low and dark as a valley; but most emphatically a valley of vision because there God was known and the prophets acquainted with his mind: Babylon, a stranger to God, is called the desert of the sea, Jerusalem, entrusted with his oracles, a valley of vision. Charles Ellicott returns to topography: if the prophet lived in the lower city the epithet fits still better. John Calvin extends the name to all Judea, rejecting as harsher the view that the city is a valley because thrown down from its height.

Two stand back from the chapter. Keil and Delitzsch note that the oracles on Babylon, Edom and Arabia are followed by this one, and that the four were joined later for their affinity rather than composed as a group, the arrangement suggested not by their dates, which run the other way, but by a storm gathering at a distance and bursting at last over Jerusalem. Adam Clarke maps the chapter instead: the prophecy against the city, the sentence against the steward, the promise to his successor, and a transition from him to the Messiah of whom he was a type, on the prophetic mode of making present things represent what is fulfilled on a larger scale later.

Why the people are on the roofs is disputed. Ellicott sees a city in excitement at the approach of the Assyrian armies, keeping its revels on the flat roofs, a customary place of concourse. John Wesley says the opposite: they went up as men do in great consternation, to cry to heaven for help. Calvin makes it disgrace: instead of being walls and bulwarks to the city, with no scarcity of men, they ignominiously turned their backs and fled to the housetops, which shows God had struck them with trembling — how else should men lack firmness to resist, but that God pursues and chases them? Gill has the streets clear, the shops shut, everyone gone up for shelter.

The noise and the manner of dying are read against each other. Gill notes that the word for stirs means shoutings and acclamations, used of joyful ones, perhaps at the festivals, unless doleful ones are meant. Ellicott takes the joyous city for the trait on which Jerusalem, like Athens afterwards, prided itself, and hears in the next clause a reproach of cowardice, since those who perished had not died fighting in battle but by the pestilence prevalent in a besieged city's crowded streets. Wesley allows famine as well as pestilence, or death in flight. Calvin draws the opposite inference: where great multitudes are gathered there was less cause of fear, which makes the panic more damning.

The fettered rulers produce a textual quarrel and a lament. Clarke finds an inconsistency: if the leaders were bound they could not flee, their binding standing earlier in the sentence; he follows a scholar reading instead that they are gone off, which the old paraphrase seems to confirm. Ellicott keeps the text and sharpens the taunt — better, fettered without the bow, the rulers having ventured a sortie and been taken without a struggle, not even drawing their bows. Wesley refers it to a later king and his commanders, fettered after their flight. Calvin turns to the prophet, who assumes the character of a mourner and bewails the fallen Church of which he is a member: what has befallen the Church ought to affect us as if it had befallen each of us. Ellicott hears one who wishes to be alone, his sorrow too deep for consolation.
5:
The day of trouble is given an author. John Calvin says the prophet again declares the Lord is behind the calamity, so the Jews should not wonder that their enemies prevail: they are fighting against God; and the doctrine cannot be so inculcated as not to be forgotten in practice, so that we are not humbled before our Judge but look to outward remedies. Charles Ellicott divides the verse: the earlier clauses paint the emotions of the coming day, the later let us hear the battering-rams, and the cry rises to the hills — either as worshippers looking to Zion, or to the high places which led their enemies to say their gods were gods of the hills and not of the valleys.

Calvin then breaks with every commentator he knows on tense. They think the discourse proceeds without interruption, the prophet making known the judgment he had just proclaimed; examining more closely, he is constrained to differ. He takes it as a reproach for obstinacy: the prophet relates a past transaction to remind the Jews how utterly they had failed to profit by earlier chastisements. Had it been a threatening the future would have been proper; the words following are past.

Elam and Kir are identified, with one emendation. Ellicott names them the chief elements of the Assyrian army invading Judah, notes that Elam, earlier named as Babylon's destroyer, was by then subject to Assyria and known chiefly for its archers, and reports Kir identified with the region near the river Kyros, granting there are linguistic and historical grounds against it. John Gill makes Elam the Persians, expert bowmen of whom a geographer reports many archers. John Wesley makes Kir the Medes, named from an eminent city of Media. Adam Clarke cannot see what a chariot of men means: the sentence has three members, the outer two naming a people, so should the middle; and since two Hebrew letters are easily confused, he adopts a correction reading Syria for man.

The advance itself is undisputed. Keil and Delitzsch trace the besiegers to the breaking of the walls: Elam has taken the quiver, Kir drawn out the shield, the choicest valleys fill with chariots, and the horsemen plant a firm foot towards the gate. Ellicott names the valleys encircling the city on the west and south, filled with chariots and cavalry ready to attack the great gate of the Assyrian inscription. Wesley notes valleys were the properest ground for chariots, the horsemen standing at the gate to assist the assault and cut off escape. Calvin will not fault the rendering a chariot of horsemen but translates literally, taking it for a military chariot, two kinds being then in use, one for baggage and one for the field.

What the discovered covering was divides them four ways. Gill offers the fenced cities of Judah, ruling out Jerusalem and the temple since neither came into the enemy's hands, and reports a view that God himself uncloaked their hypocrisy. Matthew Henry grants the point is not agreed and holds both senses: the fenced cities were a covering and, being taken, ceased to shelter, so that Judah's weakness appeared more than ever, its magazines long locked up now laid open; a scholar he names gives the other sense, that by this distress God uncloaks their hypocrisy. Ellicott makes God the one who removed the veil hiding the danger from the inhabitants and laid their weakness bare, adding that the past-tense verbs are really a prophetic present. Calvin takes the verb indefinitely and the covering more simply than any: the armoury itself, so called because the weapons were kept from public view in a sacred place. Clarke and Wesley agree on the building: the arsenal Solomon raised in the city, called the house of the forest of Lebanon not because it stood there but because it was built of its cedar.
9:
The waterworks are described in detail. Adam Clarke sets out two pools fed by springs, the upper or old one high in the city, the lower towards the bottom, and explains that when the siege threatened the king stopped the fountains outside the walls and brought their water in by a conduit cut through the rock. Charles Ellicott says the object was to stop the outflow of the streams and gather them into a reservoir, partly for the inhabitants during the siege but still more so that the Assyrian armies should find little water nearby. John Gill restricts the breaches to the stronghold of Zion, old ones long neglected rather than damage newly done by the army.

John Calvin reads the passage as a study in how men behave. During prosperity no one cares about bulwarks or instruments of war, since necessity alone arouses men and makes them active while peace and quiet make us indolent; so long as they thought themselves far from danger they disregarded the breaches, and only when a report of war arose did they grow anxious. By the city of David he means the interior part, the city being divided in two, the whole walled but the inner part more strongly fortified.

Why the houses were counted gets four answers. Gill offers a list without choosing: how many men could be spared for duty, how to levy a tax, what provisions would last, or which houses stood in the way of repairing the wall and might be pulled down for stone and timber. Ellicott takes the last and adds that a contemporary psalm bids men walk about Zion and tell her towers, while in the later siege houses came down for the besiegers' mounds. Calvin rejects the watchman theory others hold and argues that the city was examined on all sides so no building should be undefended, which the next clause confirms, since houses built against the walls in peacetime must come down in war. John Wesley wants them simply to know their own strength.

The reservoir is placed, the reproach delivered. Ellicott would render the ditch a pond, identifies it with a known reservoir between two walls, and takes the old pool for Siloam or the king's. Gill has it hold rain water against want. Clarke reads the maker not of the pool but of the visitation: God, the author and disposer of the invasion he now threatens, the same expressions being applied to him on the same occasion in a later chapter. Calvin makes the second clause the point: they gave their attention wholly to earthly assistance and neglected what mattered most, resorting to ramparts and ditches instead of to God, in whom their highest defence lay. Wesley finds an aggravation in the words long ago: they distrusted a God who had given long proof of his care.

The feast in the siege draws heat. Ellicott observes that the danger led, as in the plague at Athens under Pericles and that of Florence in Boccaccio's day, not to repentance but to recklessness, the prophet echoing the baser epicureanism of all ages in tones of burning indignation. Clarke calls it the language of everyone who has sought his portion in this life since the world began, and reports that an emperor kept an image of death in his dining-room to remind guests that life was uncertain and should be enjoyed. Calvin distinguishes: the prophet does not fault joy in itself, since an apostle exhorts the godly to joy in the Lord, but censures the joy opposite to the sadness that springs from repentance, since it proceeds from brutish indifference. Keil and Delitzsch note that so far as the calamity had gone, it was God's call to repentance. Clarke adds that the Latin read a word for voice in the closing verse, without which the sense is hard to make out.
15:
Why an oracle should turn on one official is asked and answered. Matthew Henry grants that such changes are common in courts, so it is strange so much notice is taken, and gives two reasons: as God has burdens for nations abroad that openly oppose his church, so he has for those at home who are false friends; and the whole confirms providence in events that seem to depend on the wills of princes, since promotion comes not from east or west, but God is the Judge. Adam Clarke sees less connection, granting only that it may have been delivered about the same time.

Who he was is reconstructed from his titles. Charles Ellicott reads the word for treasurer, literally companion, as a post like a vizier's, and adds that being over the house was so weighty an office that a king's son sometimes held it, almost a mayor of the palace under the Merovingians; his influence, Ellicott thinks, thwarted the prophet's counsels, and he probably led the party hoping in Egypt. John Calvin notes that he is steward here and scribe in a later chapter, which led some to think he had resigned the stewardship, though Calvin infers only a wicked envy against his successor. John Wesley reports the Jewish tradition that he was a foreigner, made likelier by scripture's silence about his ancestry; John Gill calls him an alien with no estate in the land.

The tomb is where the indignation gathers. Clarke explains that men of high rank in the east were buried in rock-hewn family vaults, and finds this man's vanity in his care to have his sepulchre on high, conspicuously placed. Ellicott makes it the last act of arrogance: having no sepulchre of his fathers to adorn, he cut one from the rock to be his own everlasting habitation, and such tombs are still found on the hills near the city. Calvin puts the sharpest question: what could be more foolish than to raise a monument in a country for whose ruin he was plotting, a foreigner longing to be buried magnificently abroad while joining its enemies? Wesley notes that stately house and stately sepulchre are fitly joined, since tombs were built near houses.

The hurling is a knot of grammar. Ellicott would render it will hurl thee with the hurling of a mighty man, strongly and effectually, while reporting a rival version, will hurl, will hurl thee, O mighty man; for cover he prefers grasp. Calvin canvasses the same options: the noun denotes not an ordinary man but a strong one, so the sense is a mighty casting out, though others take it as a vocative and hear mockery — O illustrious man, who vauntest of thy greatness and thinkest thyself a hero. He prefers the first. Gill reports the paraphrase making it the captivity of a mighty man, and rabbis who observe that a man's captivity is harder than a woman's. Clarke and Wesley agree the covering is of the face, as with mourners and condemned men.

The ball and the chariots close it. Ellicott sees a ball flung on a smooth plain where it bounds on with nothing to stay it, takes the large country for the plain of Mesopotamia, and renders the next clause thither shall go the chariots of thy glory, the shame of thy lord's house — another ostentation, since he rode in public in stately chariots such as kings used, where even judges rode mules. Gill has the verb mean wrapping or rolling, over and over to the appointed place. Calvin observes that a man so careful about his sepulchre is told he will not die in Jerusalem. On the shift from I will drive to he shall pull down, Ellicott says such changes are common, God being the subject of both. Keil and Delitzsch print the whole passage without a word of comment.
20:
The successor is introduced with little to go on. Charles Ellicott admits nothing is known of Eliakim's past, but takes the epithet my servant as witness to his faith, and thinks him in heart, if not openly, one of the prophet's disciples. John Calvin cannot fix the date, a later chapter having Eliakim steward while Shebna is still chancellor; he guesses that Eliakim was afterwards driven out by the older man's stratagems, and that Shebna, having triumphed, was punished when his frauds were detected and fled to the Assyrians. John Wesley says only that the call is by God's providence.

The investiture is taken literally. Ellicott says the words point to an actual transfer of the robe and girdle that were the insignia of office, and that father was perhaps the vizier's official title, here to be fulfilled in fact, the government paternal in the truest sense. John Gill treats the robe as a badge of office, notes that the Jews make him a priest but thinks him a civil officer; Wesley expects fatherly care. Calvin turns it into providence: all changes are directed by God, who girds kings with a girdle and ungirds them at his pleasure; and he recalls the saying that the Roman emperors were theatrical kings, since players who lay aside a king's rank become poor mechanics again.

The key on the shoulder collects parallels. Adam Clarke says that as robe and baldric were ensigns of power, so the key was the mark of office, and cites a Greek priestess called her goddess's key-bearer, noting that among the Greeks too it was carried on the shoulder. Ellicott makes it the natural symbol of the chamberlain's office, laid on the shoulder to represent its burden, and finds the same emblem in the keys of the kingdom of heaven and in the custom of admitting a rabbi by giving him a key. Calvin refuses the allegory: the expression is metaphorical, taken from the ordinary custom by which keys are delivered to stewards. Gill and Wesley look for a real ceremony of carrying a key on the shoulder.

The nail is explained from domestic building. Clarke describes eastern houses furnished, as an essential part of their construction, with pegs to hang each apartment's movables, worked into the walls at their erection, since the material would not bear their being driven in later, and contrived to strengthen them; the gold targets of the royal armoury hung on such pins. Ellicott notes the word serves both for a tent-peg and for a nail in a wall, the context requiring the second, a symbol of the support on which others depend, while the glorious throne beside it symbolises sovereignty, the pride of an obscure family. Calvin draws consolation for godly magistrates, few as they are, who may conclude God has not only raised them but established them as by his own hand.

What hangs on the nail is described with irony; whose nail falls is disputed. Ellicott paints how the new man's kindred will hang on him: the glory or the weight, since the Hebrew carries both, of his next of kin, then remoter offshoots, and at last the vessels of small quantity, cups and flagons of a crowd of retainers. Calvin infers the office is laborious if discharged properly, since God does not exalt princes to live in indolence, and that a nail suits an office full of activity and cares. Gill and Wesley have the meanest of the family take lustre from it. On the closing verse Clarke, Calvin and Wesley take the removed nail for Shebna, a repetition of the sentence already passed; Ellicott alone takes it for Eliakim, a judgment on the misuse of power just described, granting that no record of fulfilment survives, so either it was fulfilled or it worked as a warning. Keil and Delitzsch again print the verses without comment.
